1:
The four accusers are half identifiable. Gill finds nothing elsewhere about two, and doubts the guess that one father is the priest named earlier, since a priest's son would not be a prince. Ellicott places Jucal from an earlier chapter and thinks him a Levite, and observes that Shephatiah recurs in the royal house from a son of David onward, which may point to a connection; the Gedaliah here is not the prophet's later protector. Clarke labels them the faction hostile to the prophet, borrowing a scholar's name for an anti-theocratic party.

How they came to hear him is explained by his confinement. Keil and Delitzsch note that the court of the guard adjoined the palace, so soldiers on duty and people coming in could be spoken to, and there he repeated what he had held since the siege began, that resistance was futile. Calvin makes more of the irony: a prison meant to silence prophecy became its pulpit, since he was no less free than if he had walked the streets, the word of God not bound though its speaker was.

The advice was old. Calvin points out that the same thing had been said thirty years before in the temple and fixed to its doors, so nothing was new except the assumption that imprisonment had taken his tongue away; what he had long said, if it deserved death at all, was suddenly capital. Gill adds that court favours and the king's bread had not bought his silence, his confidence growing as the ruin neared; Clarke says he never wavered nor equivocated. Henry sets out the offer inside the threat: the city cannot be saved, but each man may save himself by going out early and taking his life as spoil — better, he adds, to submit to a rebuke of providence than contend with it.

Ellicott is candid about how it sounded. To anyone who did not grant the divine commission, advice to desert was treason plainly spoken, urged on men defending their fathers' city; and worse because the speaker had lately been arrested in what looked like desertion, whatever his denial. The charge of weakening the soldiers' hands Calvin calls specious but empty, glossing the hand as the organ of valour, so that loosening it means making men too listless to stir. He then raises a question against himself — whether a private man may urge subjects to break allegiance — conceding that in civil terms a prophet is a private person, however public his commission.

The king's answer is read alike by all. Ellicott sees a weak ruler conscious of his powerlessness yielding reluctant consent, and finds the scene reminiscent of Pilate. Keil and Delitzsch hear both that powerlessness and an inward distaste for the message. Calvin rejects the reading that makes the words a compliment to the counsellors' prudence: the king is confessing he has become a slave to the men who govern in his name. Gill weighs whether the phrase grants permission or states a fact about their authority, and prefers the first; Clarke abandons commentary for reproach, addressing a king who respected the prophet, feared the cabal, and sacrificed an innocent man to both.

The cistern is described with care. Keil and Delitzsch note the odd article in the phrase for the pit, explained by the need to mark a definite one when the possessor's name cannot take it, and judge it deep enough to kill. Ellicott renders the title son of the king as a court office rather than a family fact, and reconstructs the scene: a cistern drained by the siege but holding feet of black stinking mud, where enemies shrinking from the odium of an execution meant hunger to finish him. Clarke says bluntly they meant him stifled. Calvin turns it to use, holding up the world's cruelty and the servant's meekness for readers who shudder at the cross.
7:
The rescuer is closely described. Keil and Delitzsch argue from the added noun that the word means a eunuch literally, not a court officer figuratively, which fits a palace with a large harem, and meet the law against mutilation by noting that the man was a foreigner already so when taken into service. Ellicott thinks the name had hardened from a title into a proper name, as the old versions take it, traces Cushite servants in the household back perhaps to David, and adds that princes elsewhere counted eunuchs part of their magnificence. Calvin draws the implicit moral: among all the counsellors of a nation boasting its covenant, the one man who resisted was an alien.

The manner of the appeal matters to Calvin as much as its substance: had the two met by accident, a word in passing would prove nothing, but the man left the palace on purpose, which shows deliberation rather than a spasm of pity, and spoke in the gate, before an assembly, not in a corner. Clarke explains why the king sat there, the gate being the ordinary place of judgment; Gill notes the moment was well chosen, and the speech at once deferential and bold.

What was said is short and effective. Clarke infers real standing at court and a humane spirit from a willingness to speak against so powerful a group. Calvin catches the phrasing: the man would die although nobody touched him, no further harm being required, since he lay in a grave already. Ellicott renders the clause as a present, and he dies, and explains why help was otherwise impossible: his gaolers would hardly keep up the ration, the famine left friends nothing to spare, and no rescue was possible without the king. Some Greek manuscripts, he notes, put the charge in the second person, so the king himself is told he has done the evil.

The order that follows surprises them. Gill takes it for a change of heart in a king regretting the licence he had given; Calvin asks how a man who had just confessed he had no authority dared act at all, and answers that the change was an overruling from above, with the lesson that one should be brave when the occasion demands, however hopeless the outcome looks. On the escort, Clarke and Wesley both suppose force was expected against the princes; Ellicott finds thirty a large detachment to strip from a defended post and reports the conjecture that the text read three; Keil and Delitzsch, glossing the idiom as under your direction, reject that emendation.

The rags are the detail all linger on. Keil and Delitzsch locate the store in a room beneath the treasury and derive the three words for the cloths from roots meaning to drag, wear out and dissolve. Clarke doubts a wardrobe proper is meant, since eastern kings kept theirs stocked for gifts, and suggests the discarded and the insect-ruined. Ellicott calls it the lumber-room, and finds in the precaution the clearest measure of the suffering: a pit deep enough to need ropes, a body wasted enough that the ropes had to be padded before it could bear them; a clout, he adds, was once a patch of cloth, distinct from linen rags. Calvin makes the same point about the tenderness of the armpits, and commends the courage that went straight to work.

Where the rescue ended is Calvin's last concern. The prophet was not freed but moved, which was mercy rather than timidity: liberty would have put him back within reach of men his rescuer rightly judged wild beasts, and the court of the guard was the one place their fury could not reach. He would have preferred, Calvin thinks, to take him home as a guest; the prudence that kept him from it deserves praise, not the charge of fear.
14:
The meeting place is unidentified and the guesses careful. Ellicott knows an outside royal entry and a covered gallery joining palace to temple, finds this third named nowhere else, and supposes it led up from the lower city, suiting a private interview; he wonders whether the chief eunuch's chamber was used, arranged by the man who had just pulled the prophet out. Calvin explains that the king could not enter the sanctuary, so the court is meant, which had many gates and divisions. Henry reads the choice of a temple approach as respect proper in a man about to ask a word from God, and would render the request as a word rather than a thing.

Henry also names the contradiction the scene turns on. Only lately this king had handed the prophet to his enemies, and here consults him in private, one man's convictions and corruptions pulling against each other. Calvin says the respect was real and grew, and equally that it never became attention; the mind stayed suspended. Ellicott thinks the eunuch's better counsel may have had a share in the summons.

The prophet's reply looks like self-protection, and Calvin does not pretend otherwise. He states the objection at full strength — a man who had often spoken at the risk of his life now bargains for safety first, which looks like failure in the hazardous part of his calling — and answers with a distinction rather than an excuse: the prophets did not always carry an express command to speak, and where none had been given, prudence was open. Gill puts the same thing practically, that speaking could only endanger the speaker and do the hearer no good, so terms were worth settling first. Ellicott adds that the question assumes the king had approved the recent cruelty, and prefers the older versions in the second clause, which make it a statement that the king will not listen.

The oath given in return is examined for its wording. Clarke notes that the formula swears by the living God as the author of the life each man has, calls it very solemn, and marks it as the earliest recorded instance of the custom of swearing by the soul. Ellicott agrees it is deliberately weightier than the plain form, and reads the double promise as an admission: the king separates himself from the men who want the prophet dead and undertakes not even to acquiesce in them again. Both notice, as Calvin does, that the transaction is still secret, which is the measure of the man. Gill supplies two reasons: the dignity of a king swearing to a subject, and fear of the princes.

Calvin finds the oath revealing in another way. Nobody swears in advance not to take offence unless he expects to be offended; the preface about danger had told the king the answer would be unwelcome, so the promise concedes the substance before the message comes.

What is then offered is a clean alternative. Ellicott notes the emphatic Hebrew idiom, if going thou wilt go, and says the choice between surrender with life and resistance with fire is simply laid down and left. Clarke identifies the officers as the generals then returning to the siege after beating the Egyptians, their master away at Riblah. Calvin raises a question he cannot settle, whether a fresh command was given for a message so often repeated, and concludes that the Spirit probably governed the tongue where no new word had come, offering it as conjecture only. On the threat attached, he explains the pairing: hope was held out first, since the promise of mercy should have moved him, and the fire and the capture were added because hypocrites are not moved by sweetness. Neither worked, and Calvin's verdict is that the man was not an open despiser of God but neither cold nor hot.
19:
The objection is fear of the wrong people. Ellicott finds it in character: safety of life was not enough, since the deserters in the enemy camp were the prophet's own followers acting on his advice, and a king who had flinched at one man's taunts could not face their derision — perhaps, he adds, the fear went past mockery to mutilation, like an older king's before the Philistines. Calvin refuses to blame the confession, noting that the faithful commonly name their anxieties and that men who throw off allegiance treat their old master as implacably as they expect to be treated. Wesley states it plainly: the captors would hand him to the deserters.

The reply is a flat denial. Gill has the prophet guarantee that no such surrender would be made. Calvin turns it into an argument about providence: the anxiety may be laid in God's bosom, and refusing after such assurance is not weakness but deliberate perverseness, which puts out whatever light of grace was left. He insists the alternative is not open: resisting is kicking against the goad, capture certain, neither city nor temple spared.

The picture drawn to frighten him is of women. Gill takes them for court ladies and concubines left after famine and deportation; Clarke reads an actual defection in the harem, younger childless women slipping out to the enemy officers and making the taunt themselves, while wives of the first rank had no such welcome to expect. Calvin explains the figure as a part standing for the whole: fighting is not women's work and a captured city usually spares them, so if even they must walk out and surrender, the men's case needs no describing. Wesley presses the irony that a man afraid of men's insults would meet women's, and traces their reproach to the priests and false prophets who had encouraged him.

Ellicott adds a point of punctuation. The closing clause is probably to be read as a statement that the city shall be burnt, but as the text stands the margin makes the king himself the burner, which Ellicott thinks gives the true force: the destruction his own act to answer for. Gill notes that only sons, not daughters, are mentioned when the capture is later described.

What the king says next is no answer. Gill observes that nothing in it approves the counsel, the silence being itself the refusal. Calvin is harder: the fear proves he believed what he had heard, and believing it he still chose to spend his life trembling rather than end the anxiety at a stroke, which is not how a king behaves when courage is left and honour gone. Ellicott sees the vacillation running to the last, a man afraid of the prophet and more afraid of the princes; Calvin adds the pitiable detail of a ruler who could have surrendered easily but dared not, expecting to be killed in a tumult by his own counsellors.

The cover story divides them. Clarke calls it the truth and nothing but the truth though not the whole truth, holds that nothing proposed would defile the prophet's conscience, and argues that he was under no obligation to say anything that would set a weak king against powerful men or cost him his life, so he told what was necessary and no more. Calvin will not go so far. He records that the instruction was obeyed but declines to commend it, since the main thing was concealed and the reason given was not the true one; a partial truth does not wholly excuse the evasion, though the king's slavish fear of his council explains it. Keil and Delitzsch note that what the king expected did happen. Gill and Calvin close on one fact: the prophet stayed in the court of the guard, not at liberty even then, since a king who wished him free did not dare free him.
